title: Courage and grit of our Supreme Court

Contrast with US judiciary's Frankfurter-style avoidance of the 'political thicket'

stances.claim: Our Supreme Court is 'unafraid of jumping into the vortex of political whirlpools during extraordinary situations' -- unlike the US Scotus (and other countries' high courts) which prefers Frankfurter's 'political thicket' avoidance.
stances.rhetorical_move: comparative-court-courage framing (PH SC vs Scotus contrast)

stances.claim: Santiago v. Comelec (1997, per CJ Davide) and Lambino v. Comelec (2006, per J Carpio) collectively defied two incumbent presidents (FVR and GMA) seeking to extend their tenure via People's Initiative -- using PI implementing law 'insufficient and inadequate' (Santiago) and labeling the GMA PI a 'grand deception' and 'gigantic fraud' (Lambino).

Estrada v. Desierto's 13-0 legitimization (with CJ Davide and CJ Panganiban inhibited) of the GMA-Erap transition via Edsa People Power 2 is 'worse' than mere case-decision because the justices 'came out of their sacred temple in Mt. Olympus' and 'courageously slugged it out in the plains of their own volition' without waiting for a complaint -- 'unusual and unprecedented.'
stances.rhetorical_move: elevation framing (entering politics without a petition is more courageous than deciding one)

stances.claim: 'EVEN MORE COURAGEOUS, IF NOT MORE HEROIC' was CJ Davide's unilateral Jan. 20, 2001 announcement to swear in GMA at noon -- triggered by CJ Panganiban's own suggestion to administer the oath of office as 'acting president,' which the Court unanimously accepted in emergency session -- though Davide then skipped 'acting' and swore in GMA as 'president' amid chants of 'Davide, Davide, Davide' (an unauthorized deviation Davide later 'gallantly owned sole responsibility for').

Francisco v. House (Nov. 10, 2003, per J Carpio Morales) barred the second impeachment of CJ Davide because the House did not observe the constitutional one-year prohibition -- establishing that the judiciary may pass on the exercise of an exclusive congressional power 'only to determine whether the constitutionally imposed conditions, limitations, or restrictions have been observed.'

In all four cases, the justices risked serious institutional consequences -- ouster for 'grave abuse of discretion' had they lost in Estrada v. Desierto; impeachment by the House in Francisco -- making the Court's actions genuinely brave, not merely doctrinal.
stances.rhetorical_move: risk-catalog framing to underscore courage claim

stances.claim: As a member of the Court when these four cases were decided, CJ can personally 'vouch for the courage and grit displayed by the justices in tiptoeing the political minefields to uphold the rule of law and to save the nation from chaos and civil strife.'

notable_anecdotes: The Jan. 20, 2001 emergency that gave Edsa People Power 2 its legal cap: Cabinet, AFP, PNP all withdrew support from Estrada; the country was effectively leaderless ('ripe for a coup d'etat or a chaotic civil strife'); CJ Panganiban suggested to CJ Davide that the oath be taken by VP GMA as 'acting president'; the Court unanimously approved after an 'hemming and hawing' emergency session.

At Edsa Shrine at noon, CJ Davide skipped 'acting' and swore in GMA as 'president' to thunderous chants of 'Davide, Davide, Davide' -- a deviation from what the Court had authorized; the justices held several sessions over the next two days, and on Jan. 22, 2001 passed a unanimous resolution 'to confirm the authority' of the CJ to swear in GMA 'as President of the Philippines' -- Davide 'gallantly owned sole responsibility for the deletion of the word acting.'
Reference to Chapter 11 of CJ's book 'Reforming the Judiciary' for the full insider account -- turning the column into a documentary preview.
The Santiago/Lambino pair as twin defiance: FVR (1997) and GMA (2006) both had their incumbent-extension PIs shut down by the Court they themselves appointed members of.
Lambino's vivid characterization of GMA's PI: 'grand deception' and 'gigantic fraud' -- sharper language than Santiago's milder 'insufficient and inadequate.'

Francisco v. House: the House 'reluctantly obeyed' the SC after 'several days' -- a notable display of inter-branch tension successfully resolved in favor of judicial review of constitutional limitations on exclusive powers.
'sacred temple in Mt. Olympus' / 'courageously slugged it out in the plains' -- CJ's most vivid metaphor for the Court's voluntary descent into political adjudication in Estrada v. Desierto.

Closing first-person witness warrant: 'As a member of the Court when these four cases were decided, I can vouch for the courage and grit displayed' -- the line bridges CJ's status as historian and participant.

one_paragraph_summary: Following his March 11 column (A78) on Scotus's narrow Trump ruling, Panganiban offers four cases that exemplify the PH Supreme Court's 'courage and grit' in jumping into 'the vortex of political whirlpools' -- in stark contrast to Frankfurter's 'political thicket' avoidance practiced by the US Scotus. First, Santiago v. Comelec (March 19, 1997, per J -- later CJ -- Davide, en banc) shut down the People's Initiative to shift to a parliamentary system that would have let FVR continue as prime minister, ruling the PI implementing law 'insufficient and inadequate.' Second, Lambino v. Comelec (Oct. 25, 2006, per J Carpio, en banc) scuttled GMA's parliamentary-extension PI as a 'grand deception' and 'gigantic fraud.' Third -- and 'worse,' because the justices entered politics 'of their own volition without waiting for a complaint or petition' -- Estrada v. Desierto (March 2, 2001, per J -- later CJ -- Puno, en banc) legitimized the GMA-Erap transition via Edsa People Power 2 by a 13-0 vote (CJ Davide and CJ Panganiban inhibited). 'But even more courageous, if not more heroic,' was CJ Davide's unilateral Jan. 20, 2001 announcement to swear in GMA at noon -- triggered by CJ Panganiban's own suggestion to administer the oath as 'acting president' after the Cabinet, AFP, and PNP withdrew support from Estrada and 'the country was left with no leader!' -- which the Court unanimously approved in an emergency session 'after a lot of hemming and hawing'; at noon at Edsa Shrine, Davide skipped 'acting' and swore in GMA as 'president' amid chants of 'Davide, Davide, Davide,' 'gallantly owning sole responsibility,' with the Court on Jan. 22, 2001 unanimously passing a resolution 'to confirm the authority' of the CJ. Fourth, Francisco v. House (Nov. 10, 2003, per J Carpio Morales, en banc) barred the House from entertaining the second impeachment of CJ Davide within the constitutional one-year period; the House 'reluctantly obeyed' after several days. CJ closes with the IMHO doctrinal point that even when the Constitution grants exclusive powers (like the House's exclusive power to initiate impeachment), the judiciary may pass on whether constitutionally imposed conditions, limitations, or restrictions have been observed -- and the first-person witness warrant: 'As a member of the Court when these four cases were decided, I can vouch for the courage and grit displayed by the justices in tiptoeing the political minefields to uphold the rule of law and to save the nation from chaos and civil strife.'
